title: Thisness
hookLine: Duns Scotus: each thing's unique thisness is loved by God

cards: Two leaves from the same tree. Same shape, same green, the same veins branching the same way. A botanist could file them under one name and be done.
Hold them up to the window, though, and they aren't the same. One has a small tear near the stem; the other curls at the tip. This one, and that one.
A Franciscan teacher named John Duns Scotus thought that difference went all the way down, and that God sees it and loves it. He had a word for it: thisness.

teach.b: Medieval teachers wrestled with a hard question. If you and your neighbor share one human nature, what makes you you, and not just another copy of the human pattern? Some answered: the matter you happen to be made of.
He gave his answer a Latin name, haecceitas, which comes into English as haecceity, or thisness. Beyond the nature you share with everyone, he said, there is something that makes you this one.
It isn't a leftover or an accident. It's real, and it belongs to you alone. His Latin is dense and careful, but the picture is easy to carry.
God doesn't love humanity in general and each person as a sample of it. God knows the particular one. The Bible talks that way too.
In Isaiah, God says to Israel: "I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Not by category. By name.
The psalmist says, "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb," and then, "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Made by hand, one at a time.
And in John's Gospel the good shepherd "calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." Loving people in general is easy. Loving this person, with this laugh and this stubborn habit, is harder.
Some readers hear in Scotus a God who does the harder thing every time: this leaf, this sparrow, this face on the bus.

teach.h: NOT ONE OF THEM IS A COPY.
teach.b: Not one of them is a copy.

how: Christians who follow Scotus's thought, especially in the Franciscan tradition, speak of God's love for each creature in its particularity; it shows up in prayer that names people one by one and in attention to the small, ordinary things of creation.

games.q: you're a student in a medieval classroom. your teacher asks: two people share one human nature. what makes each of them this person?
o: nothing: they're copies of one pattern.
a real thisness that belongs to each one alone.
only the stuff they happen to be made of.
games.why: Scotus's answer: haecceitas, thisness. each one is itself, not a sample, and God knows the particular one.

practice: Pick something within reach, a mug, a stone, a leaf, your own hand, and look at it as if there were no other like it, because there isn't: the chip in the glaze, the crease across your palm that belongs to nobody else.
When your mind starts filing it under a category, come back to this one. If you pray, you can thank God for this particular thing.

wordCard.voice: Haecceity. Thisness: what makes each thing this one and no other, and, for Scotus, part of what God knows and loves.

orig.note: Latin, the word Scotus used: thisness, what makes one thing this one and no other.

carryVoice: Your line: this one, loved. Not a sample, and not a copy. See you tomorrow.
